factAnswerRaw: Replace it with a constrained tool that validates its own inputs
stem: A support agent has one general-purpose URL-fetch tool that several workflows use for internal documentation. A security review at a 200-person engineering org, ahead of an upcoming audit, finds the tool twice fetched unapproved external domains. What should change?

opts.t: Keep the fetch tool as is but require a human to approve any request outside the documentation domain.
Leave the tool unchanged and log every fetched URL so misuse can be reviewed at the next audit.
Replace the general-purpose fetch tool with a constrained tool that only resolves internal documentation domains and validates each request.
Write a more detailed tool description clarifying it should be used only for internal documentation lookups.

whyRight: Replacing the general-purpose tool enforces the domain boundary at the interface itself: a constrained tool that validates each request closes the gap structurally, rather than relying on a person to catch every case or a description to change model behavior probabilistically.

whyWrong.A: Human approval adds friction at the moment of use, but the tool can still reach any external domain — the broad capability itself remains unchanged.
whyWrong.B: Logging records the unapproved fetch after it already happened; it gives the audit something to review but never stops the tool from reaching an external domain again.
whyWrong.D: A sharper description changes what the model is told, not what the tool can reach; the fetch capability itself is exactly as unbounded as before.

factAnswerRaw: Keep it and add human confirmation and audit logging
stem: A finance-operations agent can issue refunds up to $500 without escalation, a capability every approved workflow uses several times daily. A new security lead, applying least privilege on sight, proposes removing the capability before the next compliance review. What should happen instead?

opts.t: Remove the refund capability immediately, since least privilege means the capability should not exist.
Keep the refund capability in place, and add a human-confirmation step plus audit logging for every refund issued.
Keep the capability, but cap the agent to ten refund actions per hour instead of adding review.
Keep the capability and add audit logging of every refund, without requiring human confirmation first.

whyRight: The refund capability is genuinely required and used daily by every approved workflow, so the correct control is not removal but human confirmation paired with audit logging — the standard pairing for a consequential capability a workflow actually needs.

whyWrong.A: Removal is correct only when no workflow needs the capability; here every approved workflow uses it daily, so removing it breaks required functionality instead of securing it.
whyWrong.C: A rate limit caps how often refunds happen but adds no review of any single refund decision, leaving the same unchecked $500 action still exposed.
whyWrong.D: Logging alone records refunds after they are issued; it supplies no confirmation step before a consequential action, which is the other half the situation calls for.

t1Clause: a capability every approved workflow uses several times daily

stem: A claims-triage pipeline already scores 92% accuracy against a stated 90% target and meets its 1,200ms p95 SLA. A vendor demo shows a larger model that would lift accuracy to 95% but roughly triples response time to 3,600ms. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Adopt the larger model and unilaterally raise the SLA to 3,600ms to capture the accuracy gain.
Adopt the larger model behind a fallback router that reverts to the current model if latency exceeds budget.
Add a reranking stage now to spend the available latency slack on additional accuracy gains anyway.
Reject the larger model; accuracy already exceeds the target, so the added latency is unpriced cost against a met requirement.

whyRight: The stated 90% accuracy target is already exceeded, so the larger model buys accuracy nobody asked for at triple the latency, breaching the 1,200ms SLA. Rejecting it keeps the system inside the requirement it was actually asked to meet, since accuracy purchased outside a stated requirement is unpriced cost.

whyWrong.A: Raising the SLA unilaterally converts a contractual latency commitment into whatever the new model needs, without the business decision that a breached SLA requires.
whyWrong.B: A fallback router adds a whole new component and failure path to manage a risk that does not exist, since the current model already clears the target.
whyWrong.C: Reranking spends latency slack to close an accuracy gap; here there is no gap to close, so the spend only threatens the SLA that is already being met.

t1Clause: already scores 92% accuracy against a stated 90% target

stem: A 300-agent support platform lets operators query a shared multi-tenant knowledge base and a third-party ticketing system. The knowledge base's vector store cannot filter at query time, and ticketing actions run under one shared service token. Select two changes that close these gaps.

opts.t: Split the knowledge base into separate indexes per entitlement tier, routed by the querying operator's tier.
Propagate each operator's identity and apply an entitlement filter inside the knowledge-base retrieval query.
Replace the shared ticketing service token with per-operator credential substitution so each action is attributable.
Keep the single shared service token for ticketing, but log which operator triggered each action.

whyRight: Separate per-tier indexes solve the entitlement gap where the vector store itself cannot filter at query time, and per-operator credential substitution makes each ticketing action attributable to the person who took it — two independent gaps, each closed at the layer that actually owns it.

whyWrong.B: Query-time filtering only works if the store can filter at query time; this vector store cannot, so the mechanism that fits a store which supports query-time filtering is infeasible here.
whyWrong.D: A log of who triggered each action is useful after the fact, but the token itself is still shared, so the third-party system still cannot attribute or revoke per operator.

t1Clause: vector store cannot filter at query time

factAnswerRaw: Streaming buys nothing; reduce total latency instead
stem: A fraud-scoring service calls a reasoning pipeline and waits for the complete response before writing a decision to its own database; it misses its 800ms p99 SLA at 50,000 calls/day. An engineer proposes streaming to fix it. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Reject streaming; it will not help this consumer, so find and reduce the slowest stage in total processing time instead.
Enable streaming so the service can begin acting on partial output as soon as the first tokens arrive.
Enable streaming and report the improved time-to-first-token metric against the stated 800ms p99 SLA target.
Reduce the mean response time across requests and report that the SLA complaint is resolved.

whyRight: The consumer here is a downstream service that waits for the complete response before acting, so streaming changes nothing about when it can start work. Total latency is what the SLA measures, so the fix is finding and reducing the slowest stage in the actual processing chain.

whyWrong.B: The service itself waits for the complete response before acting; a consumer that never reads partial output gets nothing from earlier token arrival.
whyWrong.C: Time-to-first-token is a real metric, but it is not the one the 800ms p99 SLA measures; the service still waits for the full response either way.
whyWrong.D: A mean-latency improvement can leave the p99 tail exactly where it was; the SLA and the missed deadline both live in that tail, not the average.

t1Clause: waits for the complete response before writing a decision

factAnswerRaw: 100% of access metadata with redacted payload
stem: A support assistant retrieves regulated customer records, and compliance requires provable evidence of who accessed which record for every audit. The team cannot afford full-fidelity tracing at its current 400,000 requests/day volume. What should the tracing policy capture for record access?

opts.t: Trace a uniform 2% sample of all requests so storage stays proportional to the 400,000-per-day volume.
Skip tracing for record access and rely on the application's own access logs for audit evidence.
Capture 100% of access metadata — who, when, which record — for every regulated read, with the payload itself redacted.
Capture full-fidelity traces, including complete record payloads, for every access and store them indefinitely.

whyRight: Compliance needs provable evidence of every regulated-record access, which means the metadata layer — who, when, which record — must be complete; redacting the payload keeps the audit trail itself from becoming a second store of the regulated content it is proving access to.

whyWrong.A: Compliance requires provable evidence for every audit; a 2% sample leaves 98% of regulated-record accesses with no evidence at all, which fails that requirement outright.
whyWrong.B: Application logs were not designed as an audit trail and were not evaluated for completeness; dropping dedicated tracing removes the very capability compliance is asking for.
whyWrong.D: Full payloads and indefinite retention go far beyond what proving access requires, and full-fidelity capture at this volume is exactly the cost the team cannot afford.

t1Clause: compliance requires provable evidence of who accessed which record for every audit
